structure.title: III. Descriptive Evidence: Perceptions of the Long-Term Financial Costs of Reduced Labor Supply
IV. Experimental Design (recruitment, materials, data, randomization, empirical strategy)
V. Does Information on the Long-Term Financial Costs of Reduced Labor Supply Affect Women's Behaviors?

observations.statement: The experiment is named a two-stage randomization design with a hold-out (pure control) group: a share of schools is assigned to pure control, and teachers in the remaining schools are randomized individually. Treatment and spillover effects are both estimated relative to pure-control teachers, with the hold-out justified by potential within-school spillovers and cited precedents.
observations.quote: we include a hold-out control group in the experimental design

observations.statement: Stratification variables are stated for both stages: school-level randomization stratified by school size terciles, school type and municipality type; individual-level randomization, performed inside the survey just before the video, stratified by full-time status and pregnancy. Control-group teachers are further randomized across three placebo videos.
observations.locator: Section IV.D, items i and ii

observations.statement: The spillover threat is introduced in the introduction as social learning among colleagues that could attenuate treatment effects, and is presented as the reason for the design choice rather than as an afterthought; spillover effects are then reported as a regular row in every table.

The estimating equation is displayed once, numbered (1), with separate indicators for treated and spillover individuals, individual and school-level controls and stratification fixed effects; the same equation is referenced in every table note. The choice of the teacher setting is justified by deterministic pay scales, a large linkable employer and yearly hours decisions.
observations.locator: Introduction (setting paragraph) and Section IV.E Empirical Strategy, equation (1)

observations.statement: The authors frame the study population as facing low adjustment barriers and label the context a proof of concept for the role of information constraints, setting reader expectations about scope before results are shown.
observations.locator: Introduction, paragraph on the teaching occupation

observations.statement: The sampling frame is a contact list of female teaching staff from the Department of Education. Exclusions are listed in order with reasons: teachers at more than one school, women without children, invalid responses, full-time workers (per the pre-analysis plan) and pregnant women (statutory maternity leave would mechanically change next-year hours). The unit is the teacher within a school.

The descriptive survey recruits a representative sample of mothers from German-speaking Switzerland through a commercial survey company, regardless of labor force status, with a parallel father sample; sample selection and the coding of open-text answers are delegated to an online appendix section and questionnaires to an appendix table.
observations.locator: Section III.A Survey Design and Sample
applies_to: other:descriptive survey with vignette-based belief elicitation

observations.statement: Every regression table carries a No. observations row per column, and every figure note states the N per panel or per group, together with the sample restriction used for that figure.
observations.locator: Tables I to IV bottom rows; notes to Figures I, II and III

observations.statement: Survey data are linked to Department of Education personnel records covering several years; the share of wave 1 respondents linked to the following academic year is reported, and an appendix table is cited for the absence of differential attrition by treatment status or observables. The link rate is benchmarked against year-to-year match rates for all teachers in a footnote.
observations.locator: Section IV.C.3 Administrative Data and footnote 13

observations.statement: The follow-up survey response rate is reported in the text and described as balanced across treatment and control groups, with the supporting columns of an appendix balance table cited.

The timeline is stated relative to the institutional calendar: the intervention was timed to precede the period in which teachers communicate next-year hours to principals; the follow-up ran about two months later. A reminder link sent before the follow-up and its low take-up are disclosed in a footnote.

The key moderator (cost underestimator) is defined from the baseline vignette pension estimate being above the projected value, with the complement labelled overestimators. A footnote states that results are not sensitive to this definition, that respondents without an estimate are not reported separately, and that excluding them leaves results qualitatively unchanged.

All outcome indices are built by standardizing components and weighting them with the GLS procedure of Anderson (2008); the primary financial index is described as prespecified and combines a correct-ranking indicator with a tools-demand index. Index components are additionally shown separately in appendix figures.

Short-term labor supply outcomes are defined as the change between the planned (survey) or realized (administrative) employment level for the next academic year and the current employment level taken from administrative data at the time of the intervention; employment levels are expressed as percent of a full-time equivalent.
observations.locator: Section V.C.1 and notes to Table II

observations.statement: Beliefs are elicited through an education-adjusted vignette with numerical guesses displayed in random order; wage-growth misperception is measured as the ratio of guessed salaries at two employment levels, and a guess counts as correct when within a stated bandwidth of the projection produced by the authors' calculator tool.
observations.locator: Section III.A.1 Survey Design and Section III.B.2
applies_to: other:descriptive survey with vignette-based belief elicitation

observations.statement: Several measures are incentivized and the incentive is described: numerical guesses in the descriptive survey are rewarded for closeness to projections; the financial consultation sign-up is a real choice against a lottery voucher; long-term plans in the follow-up are labelled incentive-compatible because respondents are told the answers feed an employer workforce forecast.
observations.locator: Section III.A.1, footnote 12, Section IV.C.2 and Section V.C.2

observations.statement: The baseline pension estimate in the RCT is elicited from a drop-down with fixed increments to limit response burden; the vignette is justified as anchoring beliefs about employment level, salary and child care, and the follow-up reuses a similar vignette explicitly to avoid measurement error, both with a citation to survey-design guidance.
observations.locator: Section III.A.1, Section IV.C.1.i and Section IV.C.2

observations.statement: Each main table has Panel A (main estimates of equation (1)) and Panel B (treatment indicators interacted with under/overestimator group indicators, estimated as a separate regression), rows for Treat and Spillover, an adjusted R2 for Panel B, the number of observations, pure control means overall and by group, and a p-value for equality of the two subgroup treatment coefficients.

Table notes repeat, for every table, that specifications use strata fixed effects and post-double-selection LASSO controls (with the selected list in an appendix table), that standard errors clustered at the school level are in parentheses, that sharpened q-values are in square brackets, and the three star thresholds.
observations.locator: Notes to Table I (repeated in Tables II to IV)

observations.statement: Control selection is delegated to post-double-selection LASSO fed with all pre-treatment individual baseline variables from wave 1 plus school-level controls; the candidate list and the selected list are placed in two appendix tables rather than shown as progressive columns.
Table notes define each column's outcome in words (which index, which indicator, which survey wave) and state which data wave each column uses, so the table is readable without the text.
observations.locator: Notes to Tables I to IV

observations.statement: Standard errors are clustered at the school level; the text states this in one sentence without an explicit rationale. Schools are the unit of first-stage randomization, so the choice matches the assignment level, but the link is not spelled out and the number of school clusters is given only via the sample description.
observations.locator: Section IV.E, last sentence before footnote 14
observations.quote: Standard errors are clustered at the school level.
observations.note: Tag cluster_at_assignment_level is the reader's inference from Section IV.D; no_justification_found refers to the absence of stated reasoning.

observations.statement: Multiple testing is addressed by reporting sharpened q-values (Anderson 2008) computed for each table row, printed in square brackets under the conventional clustered standard errors; stars remain based on unadjusted p-values.

Heterogeneity claims are supported by a formal test: each table reports the p-value of a test of equality of the treatment coefficient between under- and overestimators, and the text refers to significance of the difference rather than to separate significance of each subgroup alone.
observations.locator: Table I bottom row and Section V.B discussion of Panel B

observations.statement: Balance is checked at three levels and all placed in the online appendix: school-level characteristics for treatment versus pure control schools, individual characteristics across the three arms, and the same three-arm comparison within the cost-underestimator subgroup.

Attrition is analyzed twice in one appendix table: response to the follow-up survey and successful linkage to administrative records, each tested for differences by treatment status and by observable characteristics, with the conclusion of internal validity stated for the administrative outcome.

A knowledge-check question after each video documents comprehension across arms (appendix figure), and rewatch take-up of the reminder link is disclosed in a footnote; the appendix is also cited for evidence that participants engaged with the material as expected.

Before treatment effects, the RCT baseline data are used to reproduce the two descriptive patterns from the survey (top-of-mind factors and the histogram of pension estimates) and to explain why the moderator group is smaller among teachers, using a footnote to reconcile the two samples.

Robustness is a short main-text section that only points to online appendix subsections: experimenter demand effects in survey measures, choice of estimation sample and specification, appropriateness of study timing and engagement, and generalization beyond teachers. No robustness table appears in the main text.

Sample-choice robustness is handled in footnotes at the point where the choice is made: including pregnant women (footnote 9), alternative definitions of cost underestimation and dropping respondents without a pension estimate (footnote 17), each with a pointer to an appendix table and a qualitative summary.

The spillover coefficient is probed by splitting the sample into early and late survey entrants, on the reasoning that only later entrants could have learned from treated colleagues; the split appears in an appendix table and is discussed in one sentence.

The primary heterogeneity dimension (baseline prior about part-time pensions) is first shown nonparametrically with locally weighted regressions across bins of the prior, with the projected value marked, and only then collapsed into a binary split interacted with treatment in Panel B of every table.

Secondary heterogeneity along prespecified constraint proxies (ease of organizing family life, age of youngest child, gender norms) is reported in an appendix figure and summarized in two sentences as showing no meaningful differences.

The asymmetry between the two prior groups is interpreted by reference to a cited theory of losses versus gains and to the information-provision literature, with the language of consistency rather than test; the descriptive correlates of the responsive group are explicitly labelled as purely descriptive.

Effects on indices are given in standard deviation units and effects on employment as percent of the pure control mean; the administrative effect is compared with the planned increase from the survey; a back-of-the-envelope calculation using the authors' calculator translates the effect into lifetime income and pension wealth and into a share of the gender gap, with assumptions in a footnote.
Imprecise estimates are described with explicit qualifiers rather than dismissed, and the spillover estimate is sized as a fraction of the direct treatment effect.

The administrative outcome cannot capture employment outside the Department of Education; the authors bound the concern with labor force survey statistics on teachers' secondary jobs and note in a footnote that the treatment information remains relevant after occupation switches because pensions are federally regulated.

Deviations from the pre-analysis plan are enumerated in a footnote: planned additional regions dropped for implementation reasons, two baseline proxies for the moderator dropped for lack of variation, and treatment and spillover effects estimated in a pooled specification relative to pure control.

The conclusion lists two features specific to public school teachers (deterministic salary scales and flexible yearly adjustment in small increments) and calls for research on choice under uncertainty; policy scaling via employers or pension funds is suggested in the introduction.

Generalizability is addressed empirically: feasibility of half-day increments across sectors is shown with labor force survey data, and short-term outcomes of the same intervention are replicated in a small sample of pregnant women recruited through an app, with the moderator redefined from wage-growth beliefs; the small sample is acknowledged.
observations.locator: Section VII, discussion of Online Appendix A.4.4

observations.statement: Mechanisms are examined with intermediate survey outcomes at two horizons (emotions immediately after the video, stress at follow-up), engagement measures (talking to partner or colleagues, taking action), household outcomes (partner plans, fertility, satisfaction) and descriptive correlates of the responsive subgroup; the resulting account is presented as a possible explanation.
observations.locator: Section VI.A to VI.D and Table IV

observations.statement: Mechanism measures borrow instruments from cited work (an emotions question following a prior information experiment, a reduced Perceived Stress Scale). A separately registered survey about one and a half years after the intervention re-elicits these indices and is reported only in footnotes with an appendix table.

Belief updating is distinguished from salience or priming by combining three pieces: no differential learning on the ranking task, responses concentrated among those whose priors were contradicted, and the responsive group's lower financial interest; alternative household-level responses are checked and reported as absent.

Tables use three star levels, clustered standard errors in parentheses and q-values in square brackets on a third line under each coefficient; long tables are continued across pages with headers repeated; notes restate the data wave, the sample, the estimator, the control selection and the meaning of every summary row.

Three main-text figures: a bar chart of coded open-ended mentions, a four-panel nonparametric treatment-effect plot over the prior with kernel, bandwidth, top-coding, fixed effects, clustering and per-panel N stated in the note, and a raw density plot of the outcome change by subgroup with the trimming rule stated.
observations.locator: Figures I, II and III and their notes

observations.statement: Summary statistics are not in the main text; an appendix table compares the RCT sample, the descriptive survey sample, the representative labor force survey and the employer population side by side. Appendix tables and figures are numbered by appendix section (A.x.y, B.x.y, C.x.y), and an appendix table lists outcome variables with questionnaire item numbers.

The introduction previews every result block in order (descriptive patterns, learning, demand for tools, plans, administrative outcomes, asymmetry, spillovers, mechanisms, generalizability), then gives three contribution paragraphs tied to named literatures, then a roadmap paragraph listing sections II to VIII.

Order: context, descriptive survey evidence motivating the experiment, experimental design (recruitment, materials, data, randomization, empirical strategy), results ordered from learning to plans to administrative behavior, mechanisms, a one-page robustness section, conclusion; most diagnostics and robustness live in the online appendix.

Within results, self-reported outcomes come first (financial index, short-term plans, long-term plans) and administrative outcomes last, with each subsection opening on a question sentence and closing on a one-sentence synthesis.

A Data Availability section states that the code underlying the article is available in a Harvard Dataverse deposit with a DOI, which is also listed as a reference item under the authors' names; the statement mentions code only.
observations.locator: Data Availability section and reference list entry Costa-Ramon et al. (2026)

observations.statement: IRB approval (with protocol number) and AEA RCT registry registration are stated in the title footnote; the pre-analysis plan is said to be followed throughout with three enumerated exceptions in a footnote; the later follow-up survey carries its own registry ID.

Four data sources: a descriptive survey fielded through a commercial panel provider, author-run RCT surveys (wave 1, follow-up, later brief survey), employer personnel records obtained from the Department of Education for all its teachers over several years, and the public Swiss Labor Force Survey for benchmarks; an appendix table overviews the sources.

The control condition is an active placebo: videos of similar length on unrelated financial topics produced by public television, randomly assigned among three topics; the treatment video script, screenshots and an overview of the calculator tool are documented in an online appendix section.

Baseline questions, the video and the immediate outcome questions are bundled into one survey session, with the stated purpose of minimizing attrition between baseline and first outcomes; the individual randomization occurs inside that session.

gaps: No stated justification for clustering standard errors at the school level; the assignment-level link is left implicit.
No software or package named in the main text (Stata and reghdfe appear only in the replication code).
The Data Availability section covers code only; access conditions for the survey data and the Department of Education personnel records are not stated.
The online appendix (balance tables, robustness tables, summary statistics, questionnaires, pre-analysis plan link) is not part of the PDF text and could not be read.
No power calculation or minimum detectable effect discussion found in the main text.
No explicit estimand label (for example intention-to-treat) is used; effects are described as treatment and spillover effects relative to the pure control group.
Randomization inference or few-cluster corrections are not mentioned.

reading.note: All 49 pages of the extracted text were read: main text on pages 1 to 43 fully; pages 43 to 44 (supplementary material and data availability) fully; pages 44 to 48 (references) and page 49 (journal advertisement) skimmed. The PDF contains no appendix pages; the online appendix is a separate file and was not available.
